questions.q: Which of the following is a way of generating electricity, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Falling water. Wires and sockets only carry electricity to us and switches only control a device; none of them generates it.
o: Falling water at a power house
Wires that carry supply from a power house
Sockets that deliver supply to devices
Switches that start devices in a home

questions.q: Nihal's class placed a lift and an escalator under which heading?
questions.a: Transportation. The book lists train, bus, car, scooter, lift and escalator under this heading.
o: Transportation
Others
Heating and Cooling
Entertainment

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a way of generating electricity mentioned in the chapter?
questions.a: A switch does not generate electricity; it only controls a device. The other three are the generating methods the chapter lists.
o: Pressing a switch fixed on a wall
Windmills using wind energy
Solar panels capturing the Sun's energy
Using natural gas or coal

questions.q: Tara lists a geyser, a refrigerator, an air conditioner and an immersion rod from her house. Which heading of Nihal's list suits all four?
questions.a: Heating and Cooling. The book places geyser, immersion rod, refrigerator and air conditioner under it.
o: Heating and Cooling, as each warms or cools
Cooking, as each is used in the kitchen
Others, as none has a heading of its own
Entertainment, as each is used for leisure

questions.q: For the school science fair, Sana needs a source to light a small lamp in a demonstration. The science teacher gives four suggestions. Which one fits the chapter's caution?
questions.a: Cells like those in a wall clock or torchlight. The chapter says never to experiment with power supply, and that even portable generators can be dangerous.
o: Two cells like those used in a wall clock
A small portable generator kept in the school
The wall socket in the lab, with the teacher watching
An extension board plugged into the stage supply

questions.q: Aman's torch lamp glows when he slides the switch up but not when he slides it down. His friend says the lamp is faulty. What does the chapter's torchlight activity tell us?
questions.a: This is normal. In a torchlight the lamp glows in one position of the switch and not in the other.
o: Normal: it glows in only one position of the switch
The lamp is faulty, since a good lamp glows in both positions
The cells are reversed, since a torch should glow in both positions
The switch is the source of electricity and has stopped working

questions.q:
Read the statements about electricity in the chapter.
Statement 1: A wall socket is the place where electricity for a house is generated.
Statement 2: Solar panels capture the Sun's energy to generate electricity.
Statement 3: Danger signs warn that electricity can be dangerous if it is not carefully handled.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Solar panels capture the Sun's energy, and danger signs do warn about careful handling. The socket only delivers supply that was generated elsewhere and reached the house through wires.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): For experiments with electricity at school, cells or batteries should be used.
Reason (R): Electricity from cells is always more dangerous than the supply from a wall socket.
questions.a: A is true: the chapter allows only cells or batteries for experiments. R is false: it is the power supply that the chapter warns about, not cells.
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Match the heading of Nihal's list (column I) with a device the book places under it (column II).
Column I: 1. Entertainment  2. Communication  3. Cooking  4. Heating and Cooling
Column II: a. Mobile phone  b. Microwave  c. Geyser  d. Radio
questions.a: Radio is entertainment, mobile phone is communication, microwave is cooking, geyser is heating and cooling.

questions.q:
A torchlight has a lamp, a switch and cells.
(a) Which of these three is the source of the electrical energy?
(b) What is the job of the switch in the torch?
questions.a: (a) The cells (the torchlight's source of electrical energy). (b) The lamp glows in one position of the switch and not in the other, so the switch decides whether the lamp glows.
s: Part (a): the cells are the source
Part (b): switch decides whether the lamp glows

questions.q:
A windmill stands on a hill near a village in Tamil Nadu.
(a) Which energy does the windmill use to generate electricity?
(b) The houses are 3 km away. What carries the electricity to them, and what in the house takes it to a device?
questions.a: (a) Wind energy. (b) Wires carry the supply to the houses, and the sockets in the walls let devices be plugged in.

questions.q: Nihal's list has a heading 'Others' with the water pump, crane and computer. Why was such a heading needed, and what does it tell you about the list?
questions.a: Some uses, like the pump, crane and computer, did not fit the other headings, so they were put under Others; it shows that the list of uses keeps growing and one set of headings cannot hold everything.
s: Some uses did not fit the other headings
The list of uses kept growing

questions.q: Give one use of electricity in a school for each of the headings Lighting and Communication, and name one more heading of Nihal's list under which a school device would fall, with that device.
questions.a: E.g. Lighting: classroom lights; Communication: telephone or computer with internet; another heading: Heating and Cooling with a fan, or Entertainment with a television in the hall.
s: A school use under Lighting and one under Communication
Another heading with a matching school device

questions.q: Differentiate between the electricity used for experiments in the chapter and the electricity at a wall socket by their source and by what students may do with each.
questions.a: Experiments use cells or batteries, which are safe for students to use. The wall socket supply reaches the house through wires and can be dangerous, so students must not experiment with it.
s: What students may or may not do

questions.q: Mehul says, 'Electricity reaches the sockets in our houses through wires from where it is generated, so a socket is not a source of electricity.' Is he correct? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says electricity is generated by windmills, solar panels, falling water and natural gas or coal, and the supply reaches homes and factories through wires. A socket only takes the supply to a device.
s: Role of wires and sockets only to carry

questions.q: A student sorts six items into sources and devices: windmill, geyser, solar panel, immersion rod, refrigerator, falling water at a dam. Make the two lists and state the energy that the windmill and the solar panel use.
questions.a: Sources: windmill, solar panel, falling water. Devices: geyser, immersion rod, refrigerator. The windmill uses wind energy and the solar panel the Sun's energy.

questions.q: Class 7 groups the uses of electricity by purpose (Lighting, Cooking, ...). Another group suggests grouping by place (home, school, city). Give one example under each place-group and say which grouping makes it easier to spot what work electricity is doing.
questions.a: E.g. home: mixer grinder; school: projector or lights; city: streets lights or metro. Grouping by purpose shows the work electricity does (light, heat, movement), while grouping by place shows where it is used.

questions.q: Write a three-line caution notice for the science-lab door: (i) what the danger signs warn about, (ii) one thing students must never do, (iii) the only kind of source they may use.
questions.a: Danger signs warn that electricity can be dangerous if not carefully handled; never perform experiments with power supply at home or school; use only cells or batteries.
s: Line (iii): cells or batteries as the permitted source

questions.q: Suppose electricity is cut off in your colony for a whole day. Using the headings of Nihal's list, describe how at least four headings would be affected with one device each, and say which heading you would find hardest to do without. Give a reason.
questions.a: E.g. Lighting: no lights in streets or markets; Cooking: no kettle or mixer grinder; Entertainment: no television or radio; Communication: mobile phones cannot be charged; Heating and Cooling: no fan or refrigerator. A justified choice of the hardest heading (any reasoned answer).
s: Names four headings with an effect on each
Gives a correct device from the chapter for each
Chooses one heading as the hardest
Gives a reason for the choice

questions.q: Plan a five-point talk 'Electricity safely' for Class 6. It must name two ways electricity is generated, two uses with headings, what the danger signs say, which supply to use for experiments, and one thing never to do.
questions.a: Generation: e.g. windmills and falling water. Uses: e.g. a fan (Heating and Cooling) and a bus (Transportation). Danger signs warn that electricity can be dangerous if not carefully handled. For experiments use only cells or batteries. Never perform experiments with power supply at home or school.
s: A correct thing never to do

questions.q:
The science club of a school in Ludhiana has six items for its 'Electricity around us' table: a wall clock, a TV remote, a torchlight, a geyser, a mixer grinder and a room heater. The teacher says only some of them can be used for the live experiments, and the rest must be shown on charts under Nihal's headings.
(a) Which three items can be used for the live experiments, and what common feature allows it?
(b) Under which heading of Nihal's list does each of the other three go?
(c) A visitor asks the club to run the geyser live from the socket 'just for a minute' with the teacher watching. What does the chapter say?
(d) The club can either show the geyser live to impress visitors or show a chart plus a cell-run torchlight demonstration. Choose one and say what you lose.
questions.a: (a) Wall clock, TV remote and torchlight: they use cells or batteries. (b) Geyser and room heater: Heating and Cooling; mixer grinder: Cooking. (c) Never perform experiments with power supply at home or school. (d) Chart plus torchlight: the visitors miss seeing a big appliance working, but the demonstration stays within the chapter's caution.
s: Part (a): three cell-run items with the reason
Part (b): correct headings for the three
Part (c): states the rule against power-supply experiments
Part (d): chooses the chart and cell demo and names the loss

questions.q:
After the Bhakra Nangal trip, Nihal's group has these notes: (1) falling water is used at the power house; (2) a danger sign stands on a pole outside; (3) wires run from the power house to the town. The group must prepare a presentation with the parts 'how electricity is generated', 'how it reaches us' and 'how we use it'.
(a) Name two other ways of generating electricity, besides falling water, to add to the first part.
(b) Which of the three notes belongs to the second part, and what takes the supply to a device inside a house?
(c) What do the danger signs warn, and which supply may the group's model use?
(d) Time allows only one demonstration: a cell-run torchlight showing lamp, switch and cells, or a poster of the seven headings of uses. Choose one and say what the audience will miss.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: windmills (wind energy), solar panels (Sun's energy), natural gas or coal. (b) Note 3, the wires; sockets in the wall take the supply to a device. (c) Electricity can be dangerous if not carefully handled; use only cells or batteries. (d) A reasoned choice, e.g. the torchlight shows how a lamp, switch and cells work together but the audience will miss the range of uses; the poster shows the range but not how a device works.
s: Part (c): the warning and cells or batteries
Part (d): a reasoned choice naming what is missed

questions.q: The small protruding metal cap of an electric cell is its
questions.a: Positive terminal. The flat metal disc is the negative terminal.
o: positive (+) terminal
negative (-) terminal
strip that joins two cells
support that holds the spring

questions.q: Which description of a battery matches the chapter?
questions.a: Cells joined positive to negative make a battery. Joining like terminals together is not the arrangement given in the chapter.
o: Two or more cells with the positive of one joined to the negative of the next
Two or more cells with the negative of each joined to the negative of the next
Two or more cells with the positive of each joined to the positive of the next
Two or more cells with a thick wire joined to a lamp holder

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT true of an electric cell?
questions.a: The flat disc is the negative terminal, so that statement is false. The other three are in the chapter.
o: Its flat metal disc is the positive terminal
It is a portable source of electrical energy
It has two terminals, one positive and one negative
Its protruding metal cap is the positive terminal

questions.q: Why do many devices use more than one cell?
questions.a: More cells give energy for a longer time and/or more energy. The order still matters and a switch is still needed.
o: To give energy for a longer time and/or more energy
To allow the cells to be placed in any order they like
To let current pass through the lamp in both directions
To avoid needing a switch to control the lamp

questions.q: Arjun puts two cells in a torch so that the metal cap of the first cell touches the metal cap of the second. The lamp does not glow. What is the best explanation?
questions.a: Positive touches positive. In a working torch the positive terminal of one cell joins the negative of the next.
o: A positive terminal touches the next positive terminal
Two cells are too many for a torchlight to work
The lamp needs to be an LED instead of a filament lamp
The cells have lost their + and - signs on use

questions.q: Mehak looks into a remote and sees two cells side by side with a metal strip across the bottom and '+' and '-' printed inside. What is the strip's job?
questions.a: It joins the positive terminal of one cell to the negative of the next, and the printed symbols help place the cells properly.
o: It joins positive of one cell to negative of the next
It joins both positive terminals so the energy doubles
It joins both negative terminals to keep the cells cool
It works as the switch of the remote

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
Statement 1: A battery of two cells can give energy for a longer time or more energy than one cell.
Statement 2: Reversing one of the two cells in a torch can stop the lamp from glowing.
Statement 3: When cells are put in a cell holder, the negative terminal of each cell is placed towards the spring side.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three are in the chapter: more cells give energy for longer or more energy, the lamp glows only when cells are in the right order, and the activity places the negative terminal towards the spring.
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Many torches use more than one cell.
Reason (R): An electric cell is a portable source of electrical energy.
questions.a: Both are true, but being portable does not explain why more than one cell is used; the reason is to get energy for a longer time or more energy.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A torch whose cells are placed in a different order from the right one may not glow.
Reason (R): The positive terminal of an electric cell is its flat metal disc.
questions.a: A is true, since the lamp glows only when positive of one cell joins negative of the next. R is false: the flat disc is the negative terminal.
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
A torch has four cells in a row, all placed correctly.
(a) At how many places does one cell meet the next?
(b) At each such place, which terminal of one cell touches which terminal of the next?
questions.a: (a) Three places. (b) The positive terminal of one cell touches the negative terminal of the next.

questions.q:
Two cells sit side by side in a remote.
(a) What joins them?
(b) Which two terminals does it join?
questions.a: (a) A thick wire or metal strip. (b) The positive terminal of one cell to the negative terminal of the next.
s: Part (a): metal strip or thick wire
Part (b): positive of one to negative of the next

questions.q: Define a battery in the sense of the torch, and say how its cells are joined.
questions.a: A combination of two or more cells; the positive terminal of one cell is connected to the negative terminal of the next.

questions.q: Differentiate between the two terminals of an electric cell by their shape and sign.
questions.a: Positive (+): the small protruding metal cap. Negative (-): the flat metal disc.
s: Negative terminal is the flat disc

questions.q: In the chapter's activity students put the cells back in a different order and reverse one cell, then slide the switch each time. What is the purpose of doing this, and what do they learn?
questions.a: To see when the lamp glows with different arrangements of the cells; they learn that the lamp glows only when the positive terminal of one cell is connected to the negative terminal of the next.
s: Purpose: compare which arrangements make the lamp glow

questions.q: A shopkeeper says, 'The battery in a mobile phone is one cell, so the word battery means one cell only.' Comment.
questions.a: He is only partly right. The chapter says the word battery is also used for a single cell, as in a phone, but in a torch a battery means two or more cells joined positive to negative.
s: Accepts that single cell is also called a battery
Says a battery in a torch is two or more cells

questions.q: Rina says, 'In my torch the two cells face the same way in a row, cap towards the lamp, so each positive terminal touches the next negative.' Is she correct?
questions.a: Yes, for cells in a row. With both caps towards the lamp, the flat disc (negative) of the first cell touches the cap (positive) of the second, which is the positive-to-negative joining of a battery.
s: Disc (negative) of first touches cap (positive) of second

questions.q: Using the chapter's idea of a battery, show why two cells whose flat discs touch each other cannot make the torch lamp glow, and say how to correct the arrangement.
questions.a: A battery joins the positive terminal of one cell to the negative of the next. Disc touching disc is negative to negative, so the lamp does not glow. Reversing one of the two cells makes it positive to negative.
s: States the joining rule of a battery

questions.q: A toy needs energy for a longer time than one cell can give. A student proposes two cells. (i) How should the cells be joined? (ii) What is the benefit? (iii) What should be checked before the switch is slid?
questions.a: Join the positive terminal of one cell to the negative terminal of the other; the benefit is energy for a longer time and/or more energy; check that both cells are placed in the correct order (the + and - symbols).

questions.q: A torch has an incandescent lamp and three cells in a row. Each cell can be placed with its cap towards the lamp or with its flat disc towards the lamp. (a) In how many different ways can the three cells be placed? (b) In how many ways will the lamp glow? Explain with the chapter's rule. (c) If the torch had an LED whose longer wire is joined to the cap end of the battery, how many of those would work?
questions.a: (a) 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 ways. (b) Two ways: all three caps towards the lamp, or all three discs towards the lamp, because only then does each positive touch the next negative; the incandescent lamp glows whichever way round the battery is. (c) One way only, since an LED glows only when its positive wire meets the battery's positive.
s: Incandescent lamp works either way round
LED needs the single correct direction

questions.q: Meena says devices use more than one cell to get more energy. Zoya says it is to make the circuit work for a longer time. Use the chapter to decide who is right, explain how two cells must be joined, and name the one check you would do before sliding the switch of a new two-cell torch.
questions.a: Both are right: the chapter says connecting more than one cell provides energy for a longer time and/or more energy. The two cells are joined with the positive terminal of one to the negative terminal of the next. Check the order of the cells using the + and - marks before sliding the switch.
s: Meena is right about more energy
Zoya is right about longer time

questions.q:
Navjot's torch has three cells in a row: lamp, cell 1, cell 2, cell 3, spring. After cleaning, she puts them back so that cell 1 and cell 2 both have their metal cap towards the lamp, but cell 3 has its flat disc towards the lamp. The lamp does not glow.
(a) Which two cells are joined wrongly, and which terminals touch there?
(b) How many of the two joints between the cells are correct?
(c) What single change will make the lamp glow?
(d) After the repair the torch glows but gives light for only a short time on match day. Her coach suggests adding a fourth cell. Would that help, and what must she check?
questions.a: (a) Cells 2 and 3: the flat disc (negative) of cell 2 touches the flat disc (negative) of cell 3. (b) One (the disc of cell 1 touches the cap of cell 2). (c) Turn cell 3 around so its cap is towards the lamp. (d) Yes, more cells give energy for a longer time; she must place the fourth cell so that its positive touches the negative of cell 3.
s: Part (a): cells 2 and 3, negative touching negative
Part (d): more cells help, with the order check

questions.q:
A school tests a two-cell torch with an incandescent lamp in four arrangements. The cells are in a row, lamp then cell 1 then cell 2. Trial 1: both caps towards the lamp. Trial 2: cap of cell 1 towards the lamp, cap of cell 2 away from the lamp. Trial 3: disc of cell 1 towards the lamp, cap of cell 2 towards the lamp. Trial 4: both discs towards the lamp.
(a) In which trials will the lamp glow?
(b) In the trials where it does not glow, which terminals touch each other?
(c) Trial 4 has the flat disc towards the lamp for both cells. Why can the lamp still glow?
(d) A new student always uses Trial 4 and says it is just as good. Is she right for this torch? Would she still be right if the lamp were an LED?
questions.a: (a) Trials 1 and 4. (b) Trial 2: negative touches negative; Trial 3: positive touches positive. (c) The cells are still joined positive to negative, and an incandescent lamp glows whichever way it is connected. (d) Right for the incandescent lamp; with an LED the battery's positive end would now be at the other end, so the LED's longer wire would have to go to that end or the LED would not glow.
s: Part (b): like terminals touching in trials 2 and 3
Part (c): positive to negative, lamp works either way
Part (d): right for the lamp, not safe for an LED without checking the wires

questions.q: Which part of an incandescent torch lamp glows to give light?
questions.a: The filament, the thin wire in the middle of the bulb. It gets hot and glows when current passes.
o: The thin filament inside the glass bulb
The thick wires that support the filament
The metal case at the base of the lamp
The glass bulb around the lamp

questions.q: Which of the following does an LED NOT have?
questions.a: An LED has no filament. It has two terminals: the longer wire is positive and the shorter is negative.
o: A filament inside the lamp
Two terminals
A longer wire that is positive
A shorter wire that is negative

questions.q: The two terminals of an incandescent lamp are
questions.a: The metal case and the metal tip, each joined to a thick wire that supports the filament, fixed so that they do not touch.
o: the metal case at the base and the metal tip
the two ends of the thin filament inside the bulb
the glass bulb and the metal tip at the centre
two metal tips side by side that touch each other

questions.q: Ananya joins a good LED to a battery and it does not glow. She swaps its two wires and it glows. What explains this?
questions.a: Current passes through an LED in one direction only; the longer (positive) wire must join the positive of the battery.
o: Current passes through an LED in one direction only
The LED glows only when its shorter wire meets the positive
The filament of the LED mended itself when swapped
An LED glows only when its two wires touch each other

questions.q: A lamp does not glow in a circuit although every connection is firm and the cell is good. Ayesha has no tester, so she puts in another lamp that she knows works, and it glows at once. What does this show?
questions.a: Everything else was unchanged, so the first lamp is the fault; it has probably fused, which means a broken filament that stops the current.
o: The first lamp has probably fused, though it looks intact
The cell was reversed and corrected itself on its own
The switch was in the OFF position until she changed lamps
The second lamp is an LED and the first was incandescent

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
Statement 1: An LED glows only when its positive terminal is connected to the positive of the battery.
Statement 2: An incandescent lamp glows only when its metal tip is connected to the positive terminal of the cell.
Statement 3: An LED has a thin wire called a filament that glows.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Only the first is correct. With an incandescent lamp it does not matter which terminal goes to the positive of the cell, and an LED has no filament.
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In an LED the shorter wire is the positive terminal.
Reason (R): An LED glows only when its positive terminal is connected to the positive of the battery.
questions.a: A is false: the longer wire is positive and the shorter wire is negative. R is true.
o: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

questions.q:
Match each item (column I) with its description (column II).
Column I: 1. Filament  2. Metal tip of a lamp  3. Longer wire of an LED  4. Fused lamp
Column II: a. Positive terminal  b. Broken filament stops current  c. Gets hot and glows  d. One terminal of an incandescent lamp
questions.a: Filament glows when hot; the metal tip is one terminal; the longer LED wire is positive; a fused lamp has a broken filament.

questions.q:
(a) What do we say about a lamp that does not glow even though it is connected to a cell?
(b) Which part has usually failed, and what does that do to the current?
questions.a: (a) The lamp has 'fused'. (b) The filament is usually broken, which stops the flow of current.
s: Part (b): broken filament stops the current

questions.q:
(a) How can you tell which wire of an LED is positive when no marks are given?
(b) A battery's positive terminal is joined to the shorter wire. Will it glow? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) The longer wire is positive. (b) No, because current passes through an LED in one direction only, and here the positive of the battery meets the negative (shorter) wire.
s: Part (b): will not glow, with reason

questions.q: Describe in two steps what happens inside an incandescent lamp when it is connected in a complete circuit to produce light.
questions.a: Current passes through the thin filament; the filament gets hot and glows to produce light.

questions.q: Differentiate between an incandescent lamp and an LED on two points: the filament, and the effect of connecting the terminals the wrong way round.
questions.a: Incandescent: has a filament that glows; works whichever way its terminals are connected. LED: no filament; glows only when its positive terminal is joined to the positive of the battery.

questions.q: Give the full form of LED. How may an LED lamp in a torch differ from another torch's LED lamp?
questions.a: Light Emitting Diode. A torch may use one or more LEDs, sometimes of different shapes.
s: One or more LEDs, different shapes

questions.q: Bhavya says, 'An incandescent lamp glows whichever way round it is connected, so an LED will too, and there is no need to look at the wire lengths.' Is she correct?
questions.a: No. An incandescent lamp glows either way as long as the circuit is complete, but an LED lets current pass in one direction only, so its longer (positive) wire must be joined to the positive terminal of the battery.
s: LED needs the correct direction and longer wire to positive

questions.q: A lamp does not glow. You find that the lamp is incandescent, the switch is ON, the cells are in the right order and all wire ends are bare and firmly joined. Which fault remains, and how would you confirm it?
questions.a: The lamp has probably fused, with a broken filament that stops the current. Confirm by looking for the snapped thin wire inside the bulb, or by trying a lamp known to work in the same circuit.

questions.q: You must decide whether a torch lamp that can be removed is incandescent or an LED. State two tests or observations and the conclusion each gives.
questions.a: Look for a thin filament in the glass bulb: present means incandescent, absent means LED. Connect it to a battery both ways round: it glows both ways if incandescent, and in one way only if it is an LED.

questions.q: A student wrote: 'The thick wires of an incandescent lamp glow. Its metal tip must be joined to the positive of the cell. An LED has no terminals and glows whichever way it is connected. A lamp is fused when the cell inside it is broken.' Find and correct the four errors, and say which of her statements about the lamp's glowing was nearly right.
questions.a: The thin filament glows, not the thick wires (they support it). The metal tip may go to either terminal of the cell. An LED has two terminals (longer positive, shorter negative) and glows only when its positive meets the battery's positive. A fused lamp has a broken filament, not a broken cell.
s: LED has two terminals and one direction
Identifies the nearly-right idea with a reason

questions.q: You have three lamps without labels: a working incandescent lamp, a fused incandescent lamp and an LED, along with a two-cell battery and wires. Describe how you would tell them apart, and what you would see for each.
questions.a: Connect each lamp to the battery. The fused lamp never glows in either way round and may show a snapped filament. The incandescent lamp glows both ways round. The LED glows in only one way round and when its longer wire is on the battery's positive.
s: Connects each lamp to the battery
Fused lamp: no glow either way
LED: glows in one way only
Distinguishes the LED from the fused lamp by trying both ways

questions.q: Compare an incandescent lamp and an LED on four points: filament, terminals, direction of connection, and which would be more likely to fail by a wrong connection and which by a broken part. Justify your answer.
questions.a: Filament: present in the incandescent lamp, absent in the LED. Terminals: metal case and metal tip versus longer positive and shorter negative wires. Direction: no effect for the incandescent lamp, but an LED glows only with positive to positive. The LED is the one likely to fail to glow by a wrong connection; the incandescent lamp can fail by a broken filament (it fuses).
s: LED fails by wrong connection, with reason
Incandescent lamp fails by a broken filament, with reason

questions.q:
Ritvik tests three torch lamps with the same good battery. Lamp P (incandescent) glows with its metal tip on the positive wire, and glows again when he swaps the wires. Lamp Q (an LED) glows with its longer wire on the positive, but not after he swaps. Lamp R (incandescent) does not glow either way; its glass shows a snapped thin wire.
(a) Why did P glow both ways?
(b) Why did Q fail after the swap?
(c) What is the condition of R, and what stops its lamp?
(d) A Class 6 child may connect the wires either way round. Which of P or Q would you give her, and what caution would you add for the other?
questions.a: (a) An incandescent lamp glows whichever terminal joins which, as long as the circuit is complete. (b) Current passes through an LED in one direction only, and after the swap the longer wire met the negative. (c) R has fused: the broken filament stops the current. (d) P; for Q add the caution to join the longer wire to the battery's positive.
s: Part (d): picks P and cautions about Q's longer wire

questions.q:
Four groups tried a lamp with two trials each, connecting its wires one way and then the other way. All used cells from the same new packet. Group 1 glowed in both trials. Groups 2 and 3 each glowed in one trial only. Group 4 did not glow in either trial, so they blamed their cell. Group 1 then tried Group 4's cell on its own lamp and the lamp glowed.
(a) What kind of lamp did Groups 2 and 3 probably have, and what is the clue?
(b) What will Group 3 see if the longer wire is joined to the battery's positive?
(c) What does Group 1's test tell us about Group 4's problem?
(d) Group 4 can buy a replacement lamp for a model that Class 5 children will handle, and children often join the wires either way round. Would you advise an incandescent lamp or an LED? State a reason and a drawback.
questions.a: (a) An LED: it glowed in one direction only. (b) It glows. (c) The cell is working, so the fault lies in the lamp, which has probably fused (broken filament). (d) Incandescent works either way round, so wrong connection will not stop it, but it can fuse; an LED needs the longer wire to the positive and will not glow if connected the wrong way. (An LED answer with the caution is acceptable if reasoned.)
s: Part (a): LED with the one-direction clue
Part (c): fault is in the lamp, fused
Part (d): reasoned choice with a drawback

questions.q: An electrical circuit is best described as
questions.a: A complete path for current. A drawing with symbols is a circuit diagram, and a source with two terminals is a cell.
o: a complete path for electric current to flow
a lamp fixed firmly in its holder
a device with two terminals that stores energy
a drawing of the parts made with symbols

questions.q: A circuit is called 'open' when
questions.a: A gap in the path means current cannot flow. A switch in the OFF position gives such a gap.
o: there is a gap in the path, so no current flows
the switch touches both its drawing pins firmly
the lamp glows steadily even without a switch
the cells are joined positive to negative in order

questions.q: Which of the following does NOT happen when the free end of the safety pin is rotated to touch the second drawing pin?
questions.a: The circuit becomes closed, not open. The gap closes, the path is complete and current flows from the positive terminal.
o: The circuit becomes open
The gap in the path is closed
The path for the current is completed
Current flows from the cell's positive terminal

questions.q: The direction of electric current in a circuit is taken to be from
questions.a: From the positive to the negative terminal of the cell.
o: the positive terminal to the negative terminal
the negative terminal to the positive terminal of the cell
the metal case of the lamp to its metal tip
the switch to one terminal of the cell

questions.q: Which statement about the glowing of a lamp is correct?
questions.a: A lamp glows only when current passes, and current passes only through a complete path.
o: A lamp glows only while current passes through it
A lamp glows whenever one of its wires touches the cell
A lamp glows even when a gap is left in the circuit
A lamp glows once the switch has been touched

questions.q: In Swati's circuit with a cell, a lamp and a safety-pin switch, the lamp does not glow although the safety pin touches the first drawing pin. What is the reason?
questions.a: The pin must touch both drawing pins. Otherwise the gap leaves the circuit open and no current flows.
o: The pin does not touch the second drawing pin, leaving a gap
The safety pin has changed the direction in which the current flows
The lamp needs the pin to touch the cardboard before it glows
The cell has become the switch of the whole circuit

questions.q: Kabir first fits the switch next to the cell and the lamp turns on and off. He then moves it to the wire between the lamp and the other terminal of the cell, and it still turns the lamp on and off. What does this show?
questions.a: A switch can be placed anywhere in a circuit, because it only completes or breaks the one path.
o: A switch can be placed anywhere in the circuit
A switch itself produces the current in the circuit
The lamp can glow without a complete path
Moving the switch reverses the current's direction

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
Statement 1: In the OFF position of a switch there is a gap in the circuit.
Statement 2: The direction of current is taken from the positive to the negative terminal of the cell.
Statement 3: A lamp glows when both of its wires are joined to the positive terminal of the cell.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: A gap is left in the OFF position and current is taken from positive to negative. Joining both wires to the positive terminal gives no path through the lamp to the negative terminal.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The lamp in a safety-pin switch circuit does not glow when the pin touches only one drawing pin.
Reason (R): The gap leaves the circuit open, so current cannot flow.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: the gap means no complete path, so no current passes.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Match each term (column I) with its meaning (column II).
Column I: 1. Closed circuit  2. Open circuit  3. Switch  4. Direction of current
Column II: a. Gap in the path  b. Completes or breaks the path  c. Positive to negative terminal of the cell  d. Lamp glows
questions.a: A closed circuit lets the lamp glow, an open one has a gap, a switch completes or breaks the path, and current is taken from the positive to the negative terminal.

questions.q: In the safety-pin switch, (a) which part rotates freely, and (b) why must it touch the second drawing pin for the lamp to glow?
questions.a: (a) The safety pin, fixed through its ring by the first drawing pin. (b) Touching both pins closes the gap, completes the path and lets current flow through the lamp.
s: Part (b): closes the gap and completes the path

questions.q:
(a) State how the terminals of the lamp must be joined to those of the cell for the lamp to glow.
(b) Fiza joins both wires of the lamp to the same terminal of the cell. Will it glow? Why?
questions.a: (a) One terminal of the lamp to one terminal of the cell, and the other terminal of the lamp to the other terminal of the cell. (b) No; there is no complete path from one terminal of the cell through the lamp to the other terminal.

questions.q:
A circuit has a cell, a lamp, a switch and wires, with the switch in the OFF position.
(a) Starting from the positive terminal of the cell, where does the path stop?
(b) What must be done at that place so that current flows right round to the negative terminal?
questions.a: (a) At the switch, where there is a gap. (b) Close the switch (ON position) so that the path is completed.
s: Part (a): the path stops at the switch gap
Part (b): close the switch to complete the path

questions.q: Why is about 1 cm of plastic covering removed from both ends of each wire when making the circuit?
questions.a: To expose the metal, so that the metal of the wire touches the terminals and current can pass.
s: So that the wire joins the terminal and current can pass

questions.q: The switch of a safety-pin circuit and the switch on a classroom wall look very different. What do they have in common?
questions.a: Both either complete or break the circuit: in ON the circuit is closed and current flows, in OFF there is a gap and the circuit is open.
s: Same job: complete or break the circuit

questions.q: Kabir says, 'The switch is the heart of my torch because it makes the current.' Is he correct?
questions.a: No. The cells are the source of electrical energy. A switch only completes or breaks the circuit, so ON lets current flow and OFF stops it.
s: Switch completes or breaks the path

questions.q: Show that a circuit with a good cell, a good lamp and a switch in the OFF position cannot make the lamp glow, even if every wire is firmly connected.
questions.a: In the OFF position there is a gap between the terminals of the switch, so the circuit is open. A lamp glows only when current passes, and current needs a complete path. With the gap there is no path, so no current and no glow.
s: Open circuit has no complete path

questions.q: Describe a situation in which a lamp does not glow even though the cell and the lamp are both good, and the switch is ON. Give the reason in terms of the path and say how you would fix it.
questions.a: E.g. one wire end is loose, or a wire is not touching its terminal, leaving a gap. The circuit is open, so no current flows. Tighten the connection to complete the path.
s: Reason: a gap or incomplete path

questions.q: A lamp in a circuit with a cell and a switch does not glow. Give three different faults that could cause this, each in terms of the path or the parts, with one way to check each.
questions.a: The switch is OFF (check its position); a wire end is loose or not bare (check and tighten); the lamp has fused (try another lamp), or the cells are in the wrong order (check the + and - marks).

questions.q: A student wrote these steps for making a switch: 'Push a drawing pin through the ring of the safety pin so that it cannot move. Fix the second drawing pin far away from the pin. Join one wire to the first drawing pin and nothing to the second. The lamp glows when the pin does not touch the second drawing pin.' Find and correct the four errors.
questions.a: The safety pin must be able to rotate freely. The second drawing pin must be fixed so that the free end of the safety pin can touch it. A wire must be joined to each drawing pin. The lamp glows when the pin touches the second drawing pin, closing the gap.
s: Second pin placed so the free end can touch it
A wire to each drawing pin
Lamp glows when the pin touches both pins
Explains the gap and complete path

questions.q: A torch does not work. Write four checks, in a sensible order, using ideas from this chapter. Say what each check looks for, and what the common cause of all the faults is.
questions.a: Check the switch is in the ON position (a gap keeps the circuit open); check the cells are in the right order, positive to negative; check the lamp for a broken filament (fused), or an LED for the right direction; check that the connections touch and are complete. Whichever fault is found, the cause is that the path is incomplete or the current cannot pass.
s: Check of the lamp filament or LED direction
Conclusion linked to a complete path

questions.q:
Ishaan builds four circuits with a cell, a lamp and a safety-pin switch. In attempt 1 the two lamp terminals are joined by wires to the two terminals of the cell, and the switch is ON. Attempt 2 is the same but the switch is OFF. In attempt 3 both wires of the lamp are joined to the positive terminal of the cell, switch ON. In attempt 4 the lamp is joined correctly and the switch is on the wire between the lamp and the negative terminal, switch ON.
(a) In which attempts does the lamp glow?
(b) Explain attempt 3.
(c) Which one wire of attempt 3 would you move, and to where, to make the lamp glow?
(d) A friend says attempt 2's cell must be faulty. Name two checks, in order, to do before replacing the cell, and say why you chose that order.
questions.a: (a) Attempts 1 and 4. (b) Both lamp wires go to the same terminal, so there is no complete path through the lamp from one terminal of the cell to the other. (c) Move one lamp wire to the negative terminal of the cell. (d) First check the switch position (it is OFF, the quickest and commonest cause), then check the connections or lamp; replace the cell only if those are fine.
s: Part (c): move one lamp wire to the negative terminal
Part (d): two checks in a sensible order with reason

questions.q:
A shopkeeper in a market has a lamp over his name board that glows when the switch is ON. One evening it does not glow with the switch ON and a new battery pack. The electrician says the path is broken somewhere. He finds a loose wire end under the switch, tightens it, and the lamp glows. The shopkeeper wants the switch at his counter, 3 m from the lamp, which needs extra wire. The alternative is a switch on the wall right beside the lamp, which needs a ladder to reach.
(a) What kind of circuit was it before the repair, and which switch position does it resemble?
(b) Name two places in the circuit where such a break could be, using only parts named in the chapter.
(c) In the working circuit, from which terminal of the cell to which is the current taken to flow?
(d) Which switch position would you advise, and what is one drawback of your choice?
questions.a: (a) An open circuit; it resembles the OFF position. (b) Any two: a loose wire end, the switch, the lamp's connections, the cell's connections. (c) From the positive terminal to the negative terminal. (d) A switch can be placed anywhere in a circuit, so the counter is possible; drawback: extra wire gives more joints that may come loose. The wall switch needs a ladder every time. Either choice with a reasoned drawback.
s: Part (b): two valid places in the circuit
Part (d): reasoned choice with a drawback

questions.q: A drawing of an electrical circuit made with symbols is called a
questions.a: A circuit diagram. The circuit itself is the real complete path, and the tester is a device that checks materials.
o: circuit diagram
electrical circuit
conduction tester
standard symbol

questions.q: The two arrows in the symbol of an LED show that the LED
questions.a: The two arrows show that an LED emits light; the triangle shows the direction in which current can flow.
o: emits light
lets current flow in both directions
has two filaments inside
needs its terminals to touch

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a reason for using standard circuit symbols?
questions.a: Symbols only represent the parts; they do not change the real current. The other three are stated reasons.
o: They change the real current's direction
They make circuits easier to draw
They make circuits easier to understand
They help people in different countries understand each other

questions.q: Priya's diagram shows a cell with its long line towards a switch symbol in the OFF position and its short line towards a lamp symbol. Which terminal of the cell is joined to the switch?
questions.a: The long line is the positive terminal, so the switch is joined to the positive terminal.
o: The positive terminal
The negative terminal
Both terminals in turn
Neither terminal directly

questions.q: An engineer in Japan and a teacher in Pune draw the symbol of an LED in the same way and read each other's diagrams easily. Why is this possible?
questions.a: The IEC, ANSI and IEEE create standard symbols used across countries and industries.
o: Bodies like IEC, ANSI and IEEE create standard symbols
Every LED in the world comes from one factory
Every LED has a filament that can be drawn
Diagrams are always drawn to the size of the parts

questions.q: In a diagram, a battery's long-line end is joined to the base of an LED triangle, the triangle's tip is joined to a switch in the ON position, and the switch is joined to the battery's short-line end. Aman says the LED will not glow because the triangle points towards the short line. Who is right?
questions.a: The current is taken from the positive (long line) to the negative end, and the triangle points in the direction current can flow, so the LED glows.
o: The LED glows, as the triangle points the way current flows
Aman is right, since the triangle must point at the long line
The LED glows only if the switch is drawn in the OFF position
The LED cannot be drawn with a battery of two cells

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
Statement 1: In the symbol for an electric cell, the long line is the positive terminal.
Statement 2: In the symbol of an LED, the two arrows show the direction in which the current can flow.
Statement 3: Standard symbols let people from different countries read the same circuit diagram easily.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: The long line is positive and standard symbols are understood across countries. The arrows show that the LED emits light; it is the triangle that shows the direction of current.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the symbol of an LED two arrows show that it emits light.
Reason (R): An LED glows only when its positive terminal is connected to the positive of the battery.
questions.a: Both are true, but the arrows stand for the light emitted; the reason is a separate rule about connecting an LED.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
In a circuit diagram the triangle of an LED symbol points towards the negative end of the battery symbol.
(a) Can current flow through the LED as drawn? Why?
(b) In the real circuit, which wire of the LED joins the battery's positive terminal?
questions.a: (a) Yes: current is taken to flow from the positive to the negative end, and the triangle points in the direction the current can flow. (b) The longer wire (the positive terminal of the LED).
s: Part (a): yes, triangle agrees with current direction

questions.q:
(a) List the components whose symbols you need to draw a torch circuit with a two-cell battery, an LED and a switch.
(b) In which position should the switch symbol be drawn for the LED to glow?
questions.a: (a) Battery (or two cells), LED, switch and wires. (b) The ON position, so that the circuit is closed.

questions.q: What is a circuit diagram? State one benefit of drawing one.
questions.a: A representation of an electrical circuit using symbols. It makes the circuit easier to draw and understand.

questions.q: Name two organisations that create standard electrical symbols and say why standard symbols are useful.
questions.a: Any two of IEC, ANSI, IEEE. Using the same symbols across the world helps people from different countries and industries understand each other easily.

questions.q: List, in order, the symbols you meet going round a diagram of a cell, a switch drawn in the ON position and a lamp joined in one loop. Will the lamp glow?
questions.a: Cell, wire, switch (ON), wire, lamp, wire back to the cell. The switch is ON, so the circuit is closed, current flows and the lamp glows.
s: Correct set of symbols in a loop
States the lamp glows because the circuit is closed

questions.q: Isha says, 'If a diagram shows two cell symbols with the long line of one facing the short line of the next, it shows a battery.' Is she correct?
questions.a: Yes. The long line is the positive terminal and the short line the negative, so this joins the positive of one cell to the negative of the next, which is how cells are joined to form a battery.
s: Long line positive, short line negative
Positive to negative joining makes a battery

questions.q: In a diagram the triangle of an LED symbol points from the negative to the positive end of the battery symbol. Show that the LED cannot glow in the real circuit, and say what to change.
questions.a: Current is taken to flow from the positive to the negative terminal, and the triangle shows the direction in which current can flow. Drawn from negative to positive, the current would be against it, and an LED lets current pass in one direction only. Turn the LED symbol round.
s: Shows the triangle is against it, so no glow

questions.q: A diagram shows a cell symbol joined by wire to a lamp symbol, then to a switch symbol drawn with a gap, then back to the cell. Describe the real circuit in words and say whether the lamp glows.
questions.a: A cell, a lamp and a switch joined in one loop by wires. The switch is drawn in the OFF position, so there is a gap, the circuit is open and the lamp does not glow.
s: Describes the cell, lamp, switch and wires

questions.q: A student described her diagram: 'The short line of the cell symbol is the positive terminal and I joined it to the base of the LED triangle. The two arrows show the direction of current. My switch symbol is drawn with a gap, and I wrote that the circuit is ON.' Find and correct the three errors, and say whether her LED would glow even after the corrections.
questions.a: The short line is the negative terminal; the long line is positive. The two arrows show that the LED emits light; the triangle shows the direction of current. A switch drawn with a gap is in the OFF position, so the circuit is open. After correction she must draw the switch in the ON position and join the long line end to the triangle's base; then the LED glows.
s: Arrows show light, triangle shows current direction
Gap means OFF and open circuit
States the corrections needed to make it glow

questions.q: Design the circuit diagram, in words, of an LED with a battery of two cells and a switch so that the LED glows. State the direction of the cell symbols and the LED triangle, and justify them using the rules of the chapter.
questions.a: Two cell symbols joined with the long line (positive) of one to the short line (negative) of the next as a battery; the battery's positive end goes to the base of the LED triangle, the tip of the triangle goes to the switch in the ON position, and the switch returns to the battery's negative end. Current flows positive to negative, the same as the triangle's direction, and the longer (positive) LED wire is at the base.
s: Battery of two cells joined positive to negative
LED triangle points from positive side to negative side
Justifies with current direction and one-direction LED

questions.q:
A group designs a night-light with a two-cell battery, an LED and a switch in the ON position. In every drawing the LED triangle points from its base towards its tip. Drawing X: the long-line end of the battery is joined to the base of the triangle, the tip is joined to the switch, and the switch is joined to the short-line end. Drawing Y: the long-line end of the battery is joined to the tip of the triangle, and the base goes through the switch to the short-line end.
(a) Which drawing allows the LED to glow?
(b) Which end of the battery is positive?
(c) In the real LED of drawing X, which wire joins the battery's positive end?
(d) The workshop worker's LED has had both wires cut to equal length, so he cannot tell which is positive. Suggest a safe way for him to find out before fitting it into drawing X.
questions.a: (a) Drawing X. (b) The long-line end. (c) The longer wire of the LED. (d) Connect the LED to the battery one way and then the other; it glows only in one way, and the wire on the battery's positive in that case is the positive (longer-wire) terminal.
s: Part (a): Drawing X, triangle with the current
Part (d): try both ways, it glows in one direction only

questions.q:
At a district science exhibition in Chennai, the organisers can print either circuit symbols or labelled photographs on the display boards, but not both. In one diagram the cell symbol has a short line on the left and a long line on the right, joined to a lamp symbol and to a switch symbol drawn with a gap. Visitors come from many states and some are Class 5 children.
(a) Which end of the cell is positive in this diagram?
(b) What is the state of the switch and of the lamp?
(c) What would you change in the diagram so that the lamp glows?
(d) Choose symbols or photographs for the boards, give one reason, and name one thing your choice makes harder.
questions.a: (a) The right end (the long line). (b) The switch is OFF (a gap), so the circuit is open and the lamp does not glow. (c) Draw the switch in the ON position, closing the circuit. (d) A reasoned choice: symbols are standard, quick to draw and understood across states, but need to be learned by younger children; photographs are easy to recognise but show less about the connections and are not standard.
s: Part (a): the long line on the right is positive
Part (b): switch OFF, lamp not glowing
Part (d): reasoned choice naming a drawback

questions.q: Which pair contains only insulators, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Plastic and rubber. Copper, gold and silver are metals, which are conductors.
o: Plastic and rubber
Plastic and copper
Rubber and gold
Ceramics and silver

questions.q: According to the chapter, the best electrical conductors are
questions.a: Silver, copper and gold. Rubber, plastic and ceramics are insulators.
o: silver, copper and gold
silver, copper and rubber
gold, plastic and copper
copper, ceramics and silver

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT advised by the chapter?
questions.a: Handling equipment with damaged insulation is a caution in the chapter, so using such an appliance is not advised.
o: Using an appliance with cracked insulation in a dry room
Using only cells or batteries for experiments with electricity
Avoiding the use of electrical devices in wet areas
Not touching switches or plugs with wet hands

questions.q: Mahi touches the free ends of a conduction tester to a steel spoon and the lamp glows. With a wooden block it does not. What can she conclude?
questions.a: The lamp glows only when current passes. It passes through the spoon (a conductor) but not through the wood (an insulator).
o: Spoon is a conductor; the wooden block is an insulator
Spoon is an insulator; the wooden block is a conductor
Both are insulators because the tester's cell is small
Both are conductors because the wires touched them

questions.q: Rohan's tester lamp does not glow for a steel key because he left the plastic covering on the ends of the wires. What explains this?
questions.a: The plastic is an insulator, so the metal of the wire does not touch the key. About 1 cm of covering should be removed.
o: The covering is an insulator and blocks the current
Steel keys are insulators and would not let current pass
The tester's cell has changed its direction of current
The lamp has turned into an LED during the test

questions.q: Tara's father says the cracked plastic cover on a kitchen switch is 'only decoration' and can be left. Which statement from the chapter answers him best?
questions.a: The chapter says insulators such as plastics cover switches, plug tops and wires to protect people from electric shocks, so a cracked cover is a risk.
o: Insulators like plastics cover switches to protect people
Plastic covers help the switch conduct electricity better
A switch is safe as long as the wires inside are of copper
Switches are made of insulators so they never need covers

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
Statement 1: Metals are poor conductors of electricity.
Statement 2: Rubber, plastics and ceramics are used to cover wires, plug tops and switches.
Statement 3: Electricity from batteries is Alternating Current (AC).
Statement 4: Our body is a conductor of electricity.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Insulators cover wires, plug tops and switches, and the body is a conductor. Metals are conductors, and batteries give Direct Current (DC); the wall socket gives AC.
o: 2 and 4 only
1 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 2 and 4 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Copper is mainly used for making electrical wires.
Reason (R): Copper is the only good conductor of electricity.
questions.a: A is true: copper is used mainly for wires. R is false: silver and gold are also among the best conductors; copper is chosen for its lower cost and abundant supply.
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Match each term (column I) with its description (column II).
Column I: 1. Conductor  2. Insulator  3. Direct Current  4. Alternating Current
Column II: a. From the wall socket, runs larger appliances  b. From cells, powers small devices  c. Lets current flow easily  d. Does not let current pass
questions.a: A conductor lets current flow easily, an insulator does not; DC is from cells for small devices; AC is from the wall socket for larger appliances.

questions.q:
(a) Name the simple device that tells us whether a material lets current pass.
(b) A material makes its lamp glow when touched across the free ends. What does that show, and in which parts of a plug or socket would such a material be used?
questions.a: (a) A conduction tester (cell, lamp and wires with free ends). (b) It is a conductor; conductors are used for wires, switches and the connectors of plugs and sockets.
s: Part (b): conductor with a correct use

questions.q:
(a) Name the metal mainly used for making electrical wires.
(b) Give the chapter's reason for choosing it, when silver and gold are also among the best conductors.
questions.a: (a) Copper. (b) Its comparatively lower cost and abundant supply.
s: Part (b): lower cost and abundant supply

questions.q: Why should we never touch switches or plugs with wet hands? State the property of the human body involved.
questions.a: Our body is a conductor of electricity, so current passing through it may cause severe injury or even death.
s: Current may cause severe injury or death

questions.q: Differentiate between DC and AC by their source and the kind of appliance each usually runs.
questions.a: DC comes from cells or batteries and usually powers small devices. AC comes from the power plants through the wall socket and can run larger appliances.

questions.q: While testing an object with the conduction tester, why must the two free wire ends not touch each other?
questions.a: If the ends touch, current passes through the wires themselves and the lamp glows without the object, so we cannot tell whether the object is a conductor.
s: Current would pass through the touching wires
The result would not show the object's nature

questions.q: Name two parts of electrical fittings made of conductors and two things covered by insulators, as given in the chapter.
questions.a: Conductors: electrical wires, switches, connectors of plugs and sockets. Insulators cover wires, plug tops and switches.
s: Two correct fittings made of conductors

questions.q: Rishi says, 'Silver is among the best conductors, yet copper is used for wires, since copper costs less and is easier to get.' Is he correct?
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says silver, copper and gold are the best electrical conductors, but copper is mainly used for wires because of its comparatively lower cost and abundant supply.
s: Silver, copper and gold are the best conductors
Copper chosen for lower cost and abundant supply

questions.q: A conduction tester has its lamp and cell joined. Predict whether the lamp glows, with a reason, in each case: (i) wire ends touching a steel spoon; (ii) wire ends touching a plastic scale; (iii) wire ends still covered with plastic touching the spoon; (iv) the two free ends touching each other.
questions.a: (i) Glows: steel is a conductor. (ii) Does not glow: plastic is an insulator. (iii) Does not glow: the plastic covering is an insulator and the metal of the wire does not touch the spoon. (iv) Glows: the ends complete the circuit directly.

questions.q: A plug has connectors and a plug top. State which is a conductor and which an insulator, and explain why both are needed.
questions.a: The connectors are conductors, so current can pass to the appliance; the top is covered with an insulator such as plastic, which protects people from electric shocks. Both together make the plug work and keep it safe.
s: Connectors are conductors and carry current
Plug top is an insulator that protects
Both together make it work and keep it safe

questions.q: You are given a cell, a lamp, wires and three unknown objects X, Y and Z. Write a plan to decide which are conductors, showing your first step, the care needed, how you record results and what the lamp tells you.
questions.a: Make the tester with a cell and a lamp and leave two wire ends free; first touch the free ends together to check that the lamp glows. Touch the free ends to both ends of each object, making sure the wires do not touch each other. Record whether the lamp glows for each in a table. Glowing shows a conductor and no glow an insulator.
s: Makes the tester and checks it first
Touches both ends of each object with the wire ends apart
Records the results in a table

questions.q: Two plug designs are proposed for a school model. Design M has metal connectors and a plastic top. Design N has plastic connectors and a metal top. Using the chapter, decide which design works and which is safe, and give reasons. Name one caution about using a plug at home.
questions.a: Design M: the metal connectors are conductors, so current passes through to the appliance, and the plastic top is an insulator that protects people from shocks. Design N: plastic connectors would not let current pass and the metal top could give a shock. M is the right choice. Caution: never touch plugs with wet hands, or use a plug that is broken or has damaged insulation.
s: Design M works: metal connectors conduct
Design M is safe: plastic top insulates
Design N fails: plastic connectors do not conduct
Design N is unsafe: metal top can cause shocks

questions.q:
Class 7 tested a steel spoon, aluminium foil, a metal key, a wooden block, a rubber eraser and a plastic scale with a conduction tester. The lamp glowed for exactly three of the six objects. Mita must make a school-exhibition model of a plug with connectors and a top, and she can use any of these six materials.
(a) Which three objects made the lamp glow, and what do they have in common?
(b) Which of the insulators in the list does the chapter name for covering wires and plug tops?
(c) Mita suggests making the connectors from the wooden block's material. What would the tester lamp show for it, and why is it unsuitable?
(d) Choose one material for the connectors and one for the top, and give a reason for each.
questions.a: (a) The steel spoon, aluminium foil and metal key; they are metals, which are conductors. (b) Rubber and plastic. (c) The lamp would not glow, because wood is an insulator and cannot carry current. (d) Connectors: a metal such as the steel key or aluminium foil, because metals are conductors; top: plastic or rubber, because insulators protect people from shocks.
s: Part (a): the three metals and the common property
Part (c): no glow, wood is an insulator
Part (d): a conductor for connectors and an insulator for the top, with reasons

questions.q:
During the monsoon in Kochi, Anwar's mother is about to switch on a mixer grinder. Her hands are wet from washing rice, the kitchen floor is damp, and the plug top has a crack that shows the bare metal under it. She says she will wrap the crack with tape and use the grinder, since she is late for the guests. Anwar thinks they should not use it at all until it is changed.
(a) Which property of the human body makes this dangerous?
(b) What material should a plug top be made of, and what has the crack done to its protection?
(c) Which type of current does the wall socket supply, and why is it not used for school experiments?
(d) Decide between taping the crack now and using it, or waiting for a new plug. Give two reasons for your choice.
questions.a: (a) Our body is a conductor of electricity. (b) An insulator such as plastic or rubber; the crack exposes bare metal, so the protection is damaged. (c) Alternating Current (AC), which can run larger appliances; power supply can be dangerous, so students use only cells. (d) Wait for a new plug and dry hands: the chapter says never to handle equipment with damaged insulation or broken plugs and never to touch plugs with wet hands,; being late for guests is the cost of waiting.
s: Part (b): insulator, crack damaged the protection
Part (c): AC, and power supply is dangerous for experiments
Part (d): waits for a new plug with two chapter-based reasons
